title: The Monster

evidence.note: The Monster was released in 1925. The 95-year US term for 1925 publications expired at the end of 2020, so the film print has been in the US public domain since January 1, 2021.
evidence.source: Duke CSPD Public Domain Day 2021 (works from 1925)

evidence.note: The film is silent. The images are free, but any music on a modern copy is a separate work or recording and may be protected.

The film is based on a 1922 play of the same name by Crane Wilbur. Whether the play script was published or registered, and so what its US term is, was not confirmed. An unpublished play may be protected for the author's life plus 70 years, so the source play is not treated as cleared.
No dedicated modern restoration was confirmed. A faithful copy adds no new US copyright, but a new score or added titles on a restored copy would be separately protected.

editorial:
The Monster is a 1925 American silent horror-comedy directed by Roland West and starring Lon Chaney as Dr. Gustave Ziska, with Johnny Arthur as an amateur detective. It was produced by Roland West Productions and Tec-Art and distributed by Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer. A creator would want it for the Chaney performance and its early old-dark-house comedy-horror mix.

The film print is in the US public domain because the 95-year term for 1925 publications expired at the end of 2020. The trap is the layers around the print. Any score on a modern copy is a separate work. The film adapts Crane Wilbur's 1922 play, and whether that play was published, and so when its term ends, was not confirmed. Check the play before you adapt the story rather than just reusing the film.
faq: Can I use footage from The Monster (1925) in my own video?

Yes for the picture itself. The 1925 film print is public domain in the US because its term has expired. Use a copy without added music, or a score you have cleared. A recorded score on a modern copy belongs to whoever made it.
Can I remake or adapt The Monster?

Remaking the story is a different question from using the print. The film is based on Crane Wilbur's 1922 play, and whether that script was published or what its term is was not confirmed. Check the play's copyright status first. Do not assume the film's status covers it.
